articles.title: What can you automate with the X API in 2026?
articles.excerpt: As of November 2026, the X API still lets you automate your own publishing: posts, threads made of replies to your own posts, images and video, polls and direct messages. What you can no longer automa…
articles.body: As of November 2026, the X API still lets you automate your own publishing: posts, threads made of replies to your own posts, images and video, polls and direct messages. What you can no longer automate on a self-serve plan is engagement with other people. Since February 23, 2026, X accepts an API reply only when the original author mentioned or quoted you. On April 16, 2026 it removed likes, follows and quote posts from every self-serve tier. Posting costs $0.015 per post, $0.20 if the post contains a URL, and a non-Premium account stays at 280 characters even through the API. What can you still automate with the X API? You can automate anything that publishes as you. You cannot automate anything that reaches into someone else's conversation uninvited.

articles.title: Zero Data Retention Is Not a Security Boundary: How to Map Your AI Prompt Path
articles.excerpt: You can pay for Zero Data Retention (ZDR), set the flag on every request, and still have the AWS key inside your prompt tried by a stranger within hours. That is one of the results of a canary study t…
articles.body: You can pay for Zero Data Retention (ZDR), set the flag on every request, and still have the AWS key inside your prompt tried by a stranger within hours. That is one of the results of a canary study that Dragos published on November 19. HD Moore, Chief Research Officer at Dragos, and his team sent nearly two million prompts to AI services between July and November 2026. Each prompt carried secrets that existed nowhere else. These included real AWS keys tied to empty accounts, passwords, unique URLs and private git repository references. Then they watched which secrets were used, and when. Dragos's write-up describes provider breaches, resellers that kept customer prompts, and providers that ignored privacy settings. Ars Technica covered it the next day.

articles.title: How BabySea built adaptive provider selection on Databricks
articles.excerpt: BabySea is the execution control plane for generative media: one API across 80+ image and video models from 12+ AI labs, served by 8+ inference providers, running in three sovereign regions: US, EU, a…
articles.body: BabySea is the execution control plane for generative media: one API across 80+ image and video models from 12+ AI labs, served by 8+ inference providers, running in three sovereign regions: US, EU, and APAC. The hard problem is not exposing models. The hard problem is execution: deciding, per request, which provider should actually run a given model in a given region under real latency, reliability, and cost conditions. Static routing breaks down quickly in that environment, and Databricks is the intelligence layer that makes our provider selection adaptive instead of static.

articles.excerpt: This is a submission for the Presage SmartSpectra SDK Challenge. How do you know if a customer-service employee is ready to handle an angry or confrontational customer before they face one in real lif…
articles.body: This is a submission for the Presage SmartSpectra SDK Challenge . What I Built How do you know if a customer-service employee is ready to handle an angry or confrontational customer before they face one in real life? Traditional customer-service training often focuses on what employees say, but it can overlook how they present themselves. A smile at the wrong moment, a visible frown, or an inappropriate response can make an already difficult conversation worse. That's why I built Conflict Lab , a desktop customer-service readiness assessment tool powered by Presage SmartSpectra. Conflict Lab places employees in realistic customer-service scenarios where a simulated customer becomes progressively more confrontational.

articles.title: Why We Ditched Cloud Servers for In-Browser WebAssembly to Process Sensitive PDFs
articles.excerpt: If you've ever had to sign a lease, compress a tax file for an IRS upload, or merge bank statements, you’ve almost certainly used one of the mainstream online PDF tools. You know the workflow: Drag an…
articles.body: If you've ever had to sign a lease, compress a tax file for an IRS upload, or merge bank statements, you’ve almost certainly used one of the mainstream online PDF tools. You know the workflow: Drag and drop your file into a sleek browser window. Watch the progress bar say "Uploading to server..." . Wait 15 seconds while their backend converts it. Download the result while hoping their "We automatically delete your files after 60 minutes" promise holds true. For most casual documents, people don’t think twice about it. But from an engineering and privacy perspective, that traditional client-server architecture has always felt fundamentally broken for document processing. When we set out to build PDFCraft , we made an intentional architectural constraint: Zero cloud uploads.

articles.title: How BabySea uses Cloudflare to secure and control execution at scale
articles.excerpt: BabySea is execution infrastructure for generative media. That means we don't just run requests. We control how they execute across inference providers, with routing, failover, and lifecycle managemen…
articles.body: BabySea is execution infrastructure for generative media. That means we don't just run requests. We control how they execute across inference providers, with routing, failover, and lifecycle management. As workloads scale, the problem is not just routing requests across providers. It's ensuring invalid, abusive, or malformed requests never reach execution, where every mistake has a real cost. We use Cloudflare as the edge control layer to enforce correctness, security, and observability before requests reach our system. This post breaks down how that works in production. Architecture: edge as the first execution boundary BabySea runs across three regions: api.us.babysea.ai api.eu.babysea.ai api.jp.babysea.ai Each region exposes the same API surface, backed by different infrastructure.

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 21, 1676: Danish astronomer discovers speed of light — by accident — while observing Jupiter's moon Io
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 21, 1676, the Danish astronomer Ole Rømer discovered the speed of lightwhile observing Jupiter and its moon volcanic moon Io. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Nov. 21, 1676, the Danish astronomer Ole Rømer discovered the speed of light . Before Rømer figured it out, scientists thought that light travels instantaneously, or infinitely fast. Rømer disproved this almost by accident when he was studying Jupiter's moon Io . He was trying to figure out how long it takes Io to orbit Jupiter in hopes of using it as a cosmic clock. He watched Io disappear behind Jupiter and reappear on the other side. He did this over and over every 42 hours for years. To his surprise, the timing of the eclipses was not consistent. When Earth was closest to Jupiter, the eclipses happened 11 minutes early. Likewise, when the two planets were farthest away, the eclipses were 11 minutes behind schedule.

articles.excerpt: The first Starship upper stage that SpaceX ever successfully recovered won't fly again. Rather, it will go on display as a museum piece, according to company founder and CEO Elon Musk.
articles.body: The first Starship upper stage that SpaceX ever successfully recovered won't fly again. That vehicle, known as Ship 42, launched Nov. 13 on Starship 's 15th test flight. A day later, it returned from orbit, nestling softly into the "chopstick" arms of its launch tower at SpaceX 's Starbase site in South Texas. Ship 42 made it through Flight 15 in good condition, according to SpaceX founder and CEO Elon Musk , who said it "could probably be reflown with a few weeks of refurbishment." But that's not going to happen. "In this case, because it's kind of an historic ship, we're going to, I think, not take any chances with the ship and just kind of leave it for public display, because what it's done is historic," Musk said on Wednesday (Nov. 18) during a discussion at the TomorrowX Summit .

articles.title: European-Japanese BepiColombo probe arrives in orbit around Mercury today
articles.excerpt: The BepiColombo spacecraft will finally arrive in orbit around Mercury today (Nov. 21), more than eight years after leaving its home planet.
articles.body: Mercury is about to receive a robotic visitor from Earth. The BepiColombo mission — a joint effort of the European Space Agency (ESA) and the Japanese Aerospace Exploration Agency ( JAXA ) — will arrive in orbit around Mercury today (Nov. 21), more than eight years after leaving its home planet. The big moment will come after an orbit-insertion burn, which is scheduled to begin today at 1:24 p.m. EST (1824 GMT) and last for 37 minutes. BepiColombo consists of two main spacecraft: ESA's Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO) and JAXA's Mercury Magnetospheric Orbiter (MMO), also known as Mio.

articles.excerpt: SpaceX launched a classified mission for the U.S. Space Force tonight (Nov. 20), sending a mystery payload to orbit from California's central coast.
articles.body: SpaceX launched a classified mission for the U.S. Space Force tonight (Nov. 20), sending a mystery payload to orbit from California's central coast. A Falcon 9 rocket lifted off from Vandenberg Space Force Base tonight at 11:20 p.m. EST (8:20 p.m. local California time; 0420 GMT on Nov. 21), on a Space Force mission called USSF-317. The Falcon 9's first stage came back to Earth about 8.5 minutes later, touching down in the Pacific Ocean atop the SpaceX drone ship "Of Course I Still Love You." It was the 11th launch and landing for this booster, which is designated B1100.
